content.title: Showdown at VW: How the power center of Europe’s largest industrial group works
content.lead: CEO Oliver Blume's cost-cutting plan faces slim chances in politically charged supervisory board

image.author: Illustration NZZ
image.caption: Oliver Blume (top) will have to convince various supervisory board members. Among them (from left to right): Olaf Lies, Daniela Cavallo, Mohammed Saif al-Sowaidi, and Wolfgang Porsche.

content.caption: Oliver Blume (top) will have to convince various supervisory board members. Among them (from left to right): Olaf Lies, Daniela Cavallo, Mohammed Saif al-Sowaidi, and Wolfgang Porsche.
content.author: Illustration NZZ

content.text: The fate of Europe’s largest industrial group could be decided at the beginning of September. Next week, VW CEO Oliver Blume will once again ask the supervisory board for approval of his «Future Plan».

Blume already promised investors at the beginning of the year a radical restructuring of his group to make the company competitive again. However, concrete implementation remains open. Measures such as an additional 50,000 job cuts or closing four plants in Germany, which media reports say are being examined by management, are controversial.

How the future of VW is being debated behind closed doors in the supervisory board is a closely guarded secret. The group does not even publicly announce when the decision-makers meet at the corporate headquarters in Wolfsburg. However, because many supervisory board members maintain ties to the media, the dates often leak to the public anyway.
One thing is certain: Blume faces an almost impossible task.
Every German public limited company has a supervisory board. However, in hardly any company is this body more powerful than at VW. There are historical reasons for this.

Volkswagen was state-controlled for decades. The company’s origins date back to the 1930s, when Adolf Hitler commissioned engineer Ferdinand Porsche to develop an affordable car for families. After the Second World War, the company was continued by the British military administration in the occupation zone, which then placed it under the trusteeship of the state of Lower Saxony.

State influence remained firmly entrenched even after privatization in 1960. The federal government and the state of Lower Saxony each acquired a 20% stake. They regulated their control rights with the «Law on the Transfer of Shares in Volkswagenwerk Gesellschaft mit beschränkter Haftung into Private Hands.» This «VW Law» still applies today in a weakened form, even though the federal government has sold all its shares. It also guarantees trade unions rights that go far beyond the usual co-determination in other German corporations, as they had only agreed to Volkswagen's privatization under certain conditions.

Today, VW is a global group. But unlike other public limited companies, in which purely economic interests often take precedence in the supervisory board, the body at the Lower Saxony-based automaker is strongly influenced by local political considerations. In addition, unusual alliances often arise: some supervisory board members, who actually represent the capital side, argue on key issues in the same way as the employee side.
The supervisory board can be roughly divided into four camps:

The employee representatives form the largest group on the board: ten seats are reserved for them, that is, half of all seats – the usual quota in Germany for public limited companies. The spokespersons are Daniela Cavallo, chairwoman of the VW works council, and Christiane Benner, chairwoman of the IG Metall industrial trade union. Employee representatives share Blume’s insight that VW needs change to ensure competitiveness. They are open to reducing internal bureaucracy, management-level restructuring, and adjusting the product portfolio. However, they vehemently oppose further job cuts and closing entire plants. The workforce had made major concessions with the last austerity program, in which the VW Group announced job cuts at the end of 2024, employee representatives say.

jj-POkJwpGwh.text: They are reserved for 10 seats. That's half – as is also the case in other corporations organized as public limited companies in Germany.

content.text: The government of the state of Lower Saxony provides two members to the supervisory board: Minister President Olaf Lies and Deputy Minister President Julia Willie Hamburg. As a major shareholder, the state government has an interest in solid earnings and dividend payments at VW. At the same time, it would not be politically tenable for the SPD-led government to be seen as responsible for massive job cuts in the region. The state of Lower Saxony would not agree to any solution that relied on plant closures as a supposedly simple solution or curtailed the proven co-determination rights of employees, the two government representatives wrote in a joint statement.

WXro3D0yXhbS.text: The two government representatives wrote in a joint statement that it cuts back on workers.

content.text: The Porsche and Piëch families remain the largest shareholders of the VW Group, together owning more than half of the voting shares. They are represented on the supervisory board by four representatives, including Wolfgang Porsche and Hans Michel Piëch. Supervisory board chairman Hans Dieter Pötsch, a former VW CFO and now head of the Porsche SE holding company, is also close to the families. The owners understand the group’s strong culture of co-determination, and they see good relations with employees as an important condition for long-term success. However, patience is running out, according to circles close to the families. They apparently demand far-reaching changes in the group structure to reduce costs. They believed plant closures were the right signal. Pötsch recently said: «Now it is important to focus exclusively on what is necessary from a business and economic perspective. Everything else must take a back seat.» However, the Porsches and Piëchs reportedly increasingly doubt whether CEO Oliver Blume is strong enough for such measures.

tOmLL-qQNfu6.text: Together they own more than half of the voting shares.

content.text: Qatar, as the third-largest shareholder, sends two representatives to the supervisory board, including Mohammed Saif al-Sowaidi, CEO of the Qatar Investment Authority sovereign wealth fund. The desert state wants a profitable VW to diversify its own economy away from raw materials. The Qatari shareholders are critical of the co-determination tradition and the high site costs. They also recently blocked a repurposing of the VW plant in Osnabrück by the Israeli defense company Rafael.

Traditionally, the supervisory board is completed by someone who operates somewhat outside the four interest groups. Most recently, Susanne Wiegand, the former head of the defense company Renk, served as an independent controller. However, Wiegand left the board in June at her own request after only one year in office. She was reportedly frustrated by how little she could achieve on the board.

Officially, the seat is still vacant. However, the «Handelsblatt» reported on Wednesday, citing company circles, that Austrian manager Marianne Heiss could take over the position. Interestingly, Heiss had held this seat before; Wiegand succeeded her a year ago. Heiss is familiar with the VW environment. She currently serves as a supervisory board member at Audi and Porsche SE. The VW Group has not yet commented on the replacement.

Instead of the usual twenty, the VW supervisory board currently has only nineteen members – which means that the employee representatives currently hold a majority of the votes. But even if Heiss were to fill the vacant seat at the beginning of September, employee representatives would remain influential.

content.title: Clear power dynamics within the supervisory board

content.text: The «VW Law» stipulates that decisions on the «establishment and relocation of production facilities» require a two-thirds majority in the supervisory board, that is, fourteen out of twenty votes. This gives the employees a de facto veto over plant closures, which they consider a «relocation to nowhere.»

Since the two representatives of the state of Lower Saxony currently align with the trade unions, clear majorities of twelve to seven or twelve to eight emerge on many issues on the supervisory board when it is fully staffed.

This makes the starting position clear before the next meeting: Blume is unlikely to get significant measures such as site closures or further job cuts, which could reduce the group's production costs, through the supervisory board.

Legally, there are two scenarios in which the group's executive board, led by Oliver Blume, could circumvent the decision-making process in the supervisory board and instead present the austerity plans to the shareholders at an extraordinary general meeting.
After the plans are rejected by the supervisory board, the executive board would argue that the group faces an «existential threat.»

Blume would propose to shareholders a spin-off of the core VW brand as an independent company, thereby placing it outside the «VW Law.» The decision regarding closing VW plants would then no longer rest with the supervisory board.

Both paths have a catch. Under stock corporation law, they are considered far-reaching resolutions, which means that usually 75% of shareholders would have to approve them. At VW, this figure is even higher, thanks to the «VW Law.» More than 80% would have to agree. This means that the state of Lower Saxony, which owns 20%, has a blocking minority.

Minister President Lies and his deputy Hamburg have already indicated that they would not support such steps. They said: «Co-determination is not a competitive disadvantage, but an essential part of Volkswagen’s success story.» Anyone who wants to sustainably strengthen the group must not undermine employee rights, they added. The trade unions also announced protests should the VW executive board attempt to push through austerity packages without their consent.

content.title: A CEO change would achieve little

content.text: Christian Strenger is a professor at the Corporate Governance Institute of the Frankfurt School and a founding member of the German Corporate Governance Code Commission. He says: «The VW Group can hardly implement the urgent cuts anymore.»

Strenger considers circumventions of the «VW Law» that would enable simpler solutions for the group’s executive board unrealistic, arguing they would fail due to the resistance of the state of Lower Saxony. Institutionally, the starting position is clear, Strenger says: «Solutions can only exist if the representatives of the employees and Lower Saxony support them in the supervisory board.» Based on the public statements of those representatives, he does not expect the supervisory board to make groundbreaking decisions at the meeting on Sept. 4.

This would further increase the pressure on Oliver Blume. Would he perhaps soon have to step down from his post? Strenger would not expect much from that, saying: «Even a new group CEO would very quickly encounter the same resistance.»
At VW, there is only one way to the austerity plan: The group's executive board must seek compromises within the existing power structure – even if time is running out.

metadata.nzzSummaryEN:
- VW CEO Oliver Blume plans dramatic cost-cutting measures, including job cuts and factory closures, but faces broad resistance from the politically influenced supervisory board.
- The powerful board, where employee representatives and the state of Lower Saxony play central roles, blocks key initiatives due to the unique "VW law."
- Alternative bypass scenarios require approval from over 80% of shareholders, which is considered politically and legally unlikely.
metadata.nzzSummaryDE:
- VW CEO Oliver Blume is planning drastic cost-cutting measures, including job cuts and plant closures, but is encountering mostly resistance in the politically influenced supervisory board.
 - The influential supervisory board, in which employee representatives and the state of Lower Saxony play central roles, is blocking essential measures due to the special «VW law».
 Alternative workarounds require the approval of over 80% of shareholders, which is considered politically and legally almost impossible to achieve.
